The brown planthopper (BPH) (Nilaparvata lugens Stål) is a highly destructive pest that seriously damages rice (Oryza sativa L.)
and causes severe yield losses. T o better understand the physiological and metabolic mechanisms through which BPHs respond
to resistant rice, we combined mass-spectrometry-based lipidomics with transcriptomic analysis and gene knockdown techniques
to compare the lipidomes of BPHs feeding on either of the two resistant (NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9) plants or a wild-type, BPH
susceptible (931 1) plant. Insects that were fed on resistant rice transformed triglyceride (TG) to phosphatidylcholine (PC) and
digalactosyldiacylglycerol (DGDG), with these lipid classes showing significant alterations in fatty acid composition. Moreover ,
the insects that were fed on resistant rice were characterized by prominent expression changes in genes involved in lipid
metabolism processes. Knockdown of the NlBmm gene, which encodes a lipase that regulates the mobilization of lipid reserves,
significantly increased TG content and feeding performance of BPHs on resistant plants relative to dsGFP-injected BPHs. Our
study provides the first detailed description of lipid changes in BPHs fed on resistant and susceptible rice genotypes. Results
from BPHs fed on resistant rice plants reveal that these insects can accelerate TG mobilization to provide energy for cell
proliferation, body maintenance, growth and oviposition.

INTRODUCTION
The brown planthopper (BPH), Nilaparvata lugens (Stål)
(Hemiptera: Delphacidae), is a piercing-sucking insect that
can damage rice both directly by ingesting sap from the
phloem and indirectly by transmitting viral diseases (Sōga-
wa, 1982; Hibino, 1996; Hao et al., 2008; W ang et al., 2008).
BPHs migrate long distances—upwards of several hundred
kilometers across diff erent countries—cause heavy yield
losses every year (Cheng et al., 2013a). BPH resistance
genes have been identified and successfully integrated into
rice breeding programs (Du et al., 2009; Cheng et al., 2013b;
T amura et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; W ang et al., 2015b; Ren
et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2018). Hence, the
cultivation of BPH resistant rice varieties has been proven to
be an ef fective and environmentally-friendly method for
minimizing the damage caused by BPHs (V elusamy et al.,
1995; Fujita et al., 2012).
Previous experiments have shown that BPHs fed on re-
sistant rice demonstrated slower growth rates, higher mor -

tality and lower fecundity than BPHs fed on susceptible rice
cultivars (Sogawa and Pathak, 1970). There is evidence
showing that BPHs respond diffe rently to various rice vari-
eties at the metabolic level. A metabolomic analysis of
biotype 1 BPHs revealed that insects fed on the resistant rice
strain YHY15 demonstrated lower levels of most amino
acids, but higher levels of urea, succinic acid and malic acid
than insects fed on the susceptible rice strain TN1 (Peng et
al., 2016). Furthermore, insects that were fed on resistant B5
and susceptible TN1 plants could be diffe rentiated based on
amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, nucleotides and TCA cycle
intermediates (Liu et al., 2017). Another study compared the
metabolic responses among BPHs fed on resistant IR56 and
susceptible TN1 rice plants, and the results revealed sig-
nificantly lower concentrations of most sugars and certain
essential amino acids, but elevated levels of most free fatty
acids (FF As) and certain non-essential amino acids in the
BPHs fed on the resistant IR56 plants (Y ue et al., 2019).
Gene expression in BPHs can also be af fected by the host
genotype. Ji et al. (2013) compared the salivary gland tran-
scriptomes of two BPH populations maintained on either
susceptible rice variety TN1 (TN1-population) or resistant
rice variety Mudgo containing Bph1 (M-population). The
results suggested that genes involved in metabolism, diges-
tion and absorption, and salivary secretion might be related
to insect virulence. T ranscriptome-wide analyses of the fat
bodies revealed diffe rential expression of genes related to
metabolism and immunity in the TN1- and M-populations
(Y u et al., 2014). The BPHs of TN1- and M-populations were
allowed to feed on Mudgo or TN1 plants, transcriptome
analyses revealed diff erential regulation of genes involved in
cuticle formation, detoxification, metabolite transport, di-
gestion, RNA processing, lipid or fatty acid metabolism,
proteolysis and insulin signaling (W an et al., 2019). More-
over , genes related to carbohydrate metabolism were up-
regulated in the salivary glands of BPHs fed on resistant rice
B5 in comparison to insects fed on susceptible rice TN1
(W ang et al., 2015a). Zhang et al. (2019) also reported that
genes involved in BPH starvation response, detoxification,
apoptosis and autophagy were up-regulated in BPHs that
were fed on a resistant Bph6-transgenic line in comparison to
insects fed on susceptible wild type Nipponbare plants
(Zhang et al., 2019). Furthermore, the transcription—along
with enzymatic activity—of a neutral ceramidase,
NlnCDase, increased once BPHs were fed on resistant rice
varieties (Shi et al., 2018). However , the lipidomic changes
associated with BPH insects fed on resistant and susceptible
rice plants have not been studied before, while the sig-
nificance of various lipids in BPH-host interactions has also
received limited attention.
Insects primarily store lipids in adipocytes, also referred to
as fat bodies, with triglycerides (TGs) accounting for ap-
proximately 90% of the total fat body lipids (Law and W ells,
1989; Arrese and W ells, 1997). TGs serve as an important
source of energy , and are vital for insects to meet the energy
demands of long-distance flight as well as reproduction,
development and starvation stress (Beenakkers et al., 1985;
Arrese and Soulages, 2010). Therefore, insects keep fat
storage levels and ener gy homeostasis in dynamic equili-
brium through the delicate balance between lipogenesis and
lipolysis. These processes are essential to provide an acute
energy supply to physiological processes during an energy
shortage (Grönke et al., 2007). TGs also serve as a precursor
in phospholipid biosynthesis (Cook and Spence, 1985).
Other lipids, such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), are major
membrane constituents and play important roles in signal
transduction as precursors to several second messenger
molecules (T ronchère et al., 1994). PC has also been im-
plicated in the control of cell growth and survival (Jack-
owski, 1994; Cui et al., 1996). Moreover , digalactosyl-
diacylglycerol (DGDG), along with monogalactosyldiacy-
lglycerol (MGDG) and PC, are major components of thyla-
koids, the membrane component of chloroplasts. As reported
by Christeller et al. (201 1), folivorous lepidopteran larvae
might utilize these lipid sources to synthesize essential
polyunsaturated fatty acids or as an abundant energy source
for growth. It is important to state that the lipids within in-
sects are in a constant state of flux, and are constantly being
converted into other forms (Moessinger et al., 2014). Lipo-
lysis is initiated by TG lipases, which catabolize TG to
generate diacylglycerol (DG), a key intermediate in lipid
metabolism and a precursor of membrane and complex lipids
(Bagnato and Igal, 2003; Carrasco and Mérida, 2007). TG
stored in human fibroblasts can be mobilized to synthesize
phospholipids and the TG-derived mono- or diacylglycerol
intermediate can be recycled to PC (Igal and Coleman,
1996). DG can also be utilized in galactolipid synthesis.
MGDG synthases catalyze the transfer of one galactose from
uridine diphosphate (UDP)-galactose (UDP-Gal) to DG,
while DGDG synthases catalyze the transfer of a galactose
from UDP-Gal to MGDG in order to form DGDG (Naka-
mura et al., 2003; Hölzl and Dörmann, 2019).
Even though lipid metabolism is vital to insects, there is a
limited knowledge base concerning lipid composition and
transformation in BPHs. Only incomplete information about
how BPH-plant interactions af fect the BPH lipidome cur -
rently exists. Fortunately , new lipidomics approaches based
on mass spectrometry make this possible. Previous meta-
bolomics studies in BPH have only investigated changes in a
few FF As using GC-MS (Liu et al., 2017; Y ue et al., 2019),
while comprehensive lipidomics information at the species
level remains obscure due to intricate lipid structures and
masses of isomers and isobars (Cajka and Fiehn, 2014; Junot
et al., 2014; Narváez-Rivas and Zhang, 2016). For this rea-
son, research should focus on developing an accurate and
sensitive technique for quantifying lipids in BPHs to further

understand how host resistance influences lipid metabolism
in this potent pest. Hybrid Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass
spectrometry has been increasingly used to profile lipids
from diverse matrices such as suspension cells, soft tissue
and termites because of its impressive sensitivity , resolution
and mass accuracy (Breitkopf et al., 2015; Breitkopf et al.,
2017; Chen et al., 2018b; Jirošová et al., 2018).
In this study , we combined UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap
mass spectrometry with genetic expression analyses to ex-
plore lipid regulation in BPH insects fed on three different
rice plants, namely , cultivar 931 1 and the resistant near-
isogenic lines (NILs) NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9. Cultivar
931 1 is a popular , high-yield variety which is susceptible to
BPH infestation. NIL-Bph6 includes the resistance gene
Bph6, while NIL-Bph9 carries Bph9 in the 931 1 genetic
background. As such, both are resistant to BPH (Zhao et al.,
2016; Guo et al., 2018). Our results reveal that the host plant
genotype was associated with extensive changes to the lipid
metabolism of BPH insects.

The performance of BPH insects decr eased when they
wer e fed on resistant rice plants
The BPH resistance of the near -isogenic lines NIL-Bph6 and
NIL-Bph9 was first evaluated at the seedling stage. While the
wild-type 931 1 plants at this stage died completely , the NIL-
Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants grew normally and showed
strong BPH resistance (Figure 1A). W e then investigated the
performance of BPHs across the three genotypes of rice
plants. In the two-host choice tests, the number of BPHs on
NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9, relative to 931 1, declined sig-
nificantly from 24 h to 96 h after BPH release (Figure 1B and
C). When adult BPH insects were forced to feed on NIL-
Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants, honeydew excretion—an in-
dicator of how much the insects are feeding—markedly re-
duced compared to the values measured for insects fed on
931 1 plants (Figure 1D). Hence, the NIL plants inhibited
BPH feeding. In subsequent experiments, BPH insects with
similar body sizes were allowed to feed on the three geno-
types of rice plants for 48 h. Both nymph and adult insects
fed on NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants grew slower and were
much thinner when compared to those fed on 931 1 plants
(Figure 1E and Figure S1A and B in Supporting Informa-
tion). BPH nymphs that were fed on NIL-Bph6 and NIL-
Bph9 plants showed significantly higher mortality rates
(26% and 18.44%, respectively) than those fed on 931 1
(8.44%) plants (Figure 1F). Furthermore, we also compared
the number of eggs laid by females that had been constrained
to NIL-Bph6, NIL-Bph9, or 931 1 rice plants. The females
constrained to NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants showed a
pronounced reduction in oviposition (39.2% and 33.1%, re-
spectively) when compared to females constrained to 931 1
plants (Figure S1C in Supporting Information). Our results
demonstrated that the NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants ex-
hibited both antixenotic and antibiotic ef fects, which in-
hibited the feeding, growth, survival and development of
BPH insects.
Insects that wer e fed on r esistant plants demonstrated
decr eased lipid contents
The decreased feeding rates observed among BPHs on re-
sistant NIL rice plants resulted in slower growth and thinner
insects. W e dissected the bodies of insects fed on different
rice plants to compare the lipid contents of BPHs having
undergone different treatments. The abdomens of WT in-
sects fed on susceptible rice plants were filled with hyper -
trophied fat bodies, while the B6 and B9 insects, which
were fed on the resistant plants NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9,
respectively , showed far smaller fat bodies in the abdomen
relative to WT insects (Figure 2A). The results suggest that
BPHs fed on NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants may be
characterized by abnormal lipid metabolism and deposition.
T o confirm this, we measured the lipid contents in the fat
bodies of BPHs that were fed on resistant and susceptible
rice plants. W e stained the intracellular lipid droplets with
Nile red and evaluated the relative lipid storage within the
fat bodies. W e observed that the fat bodies of insects fed on
resistant rice (NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9) exhibited smaller
lipid droplets (which were also characterized by lower
densities) than those of insects fed on susceptible rice
(931 1) (Figure 2B). The experiments revealed that lipid
storage in insects fed on NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 de-
creased by 45.06% and 35.88%, respectively , compared to
that in insects fed on 931 1 (Figure 2C). In insects, TGs are
the primary form of lipid storage in fat bodies (Grönke et
al., 2005; Arrese and Soulages, 2010). The TG content in
BPH insects fed on resistant rice (NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9)
reduced 48.3% and 27.8%, respectively , compared to that in
insects fed on susceptible rice (931 1) (Figure 2D). The in-
sects fed on susceptible rice showed significant increases in
body weights and TG contents; however , insects rarely
exhibited variations in body weight and significant de-
creases in TG contents after feeding on resistant rice for 48
h. These observations indicate that plant host resistance to
BPH infestation significantly influences the lipid metabo-
lism of BPHs, as well as lipid deposition in fat bodies.
Overall lipid composition was affected by BPH re-
sistance
T o clarify how BPH resistance af fects the lipid composi-
tion in BPH insects, we performed a UHPLC-MS-based
lipidomic analysis of BPH insects that were fed on dif-

ferent genotypes of rice for 48 h (Figure S2 in Supporting
Information). A total of 828 lipid species representing
three main categories—glycerophospholipids (GP), gly-
cerolipids (GL) and sphingolipids (SP)—were identified
in the insects ( T ables S1 and S2 in Supporting Informa-
tion). The identified lipids belonged to 29 dif ferent lipid
classes (T able S3 in Supporting Information), with lipids
most often representing the PC, phosphatidylethanolamine
(PE), TG, phosphatidylserine (PS) and sphingomyelin
(SM) lipid classes (Figure S3A in Supporting Informa-
tion). The length of detected fatty acyl chains varied from
4 to 66 carbons, with the number of double bonds ranging
from 0 to 1 1 (T able S4 in Supporting Information). Li-
noleate (18:2) and oleate (18:1) were the most abundant
fatty acids detected from the samples (Figure S3B in
Supporting Information) .
T he lipid compositions of BPH insects fed on three dif-
ferent genotypes of rice are presented in Figure 3 A, with
detailed information provided in T able S5 in Supporting
Information. BPHs fed on NIL- Bph6 and NIL- Bph9 had
lower TG contents (7.42% and 1 1.10%, respectively) than
insects fed on 931 1 rice (15.53%). Conversely , BPHs fed on
resistant plants had higher PC contents than BPHs fed on
susceptible plants, i.e., 60.51% in B6 and 57.39% in B9
compared to 52.83% in WT . In addition, B6 and B9 insects
showed a substantial increase in DGDG (0.25% in B6 and
0.28% in B9), a minor lipid class, relative to WT insects
(0.09% in WT). T otal TG content decreased by 8.1 1% and
4.43% in B6 and B9, compared to that in WT . The decrease
was mostly occupied by PC and DGDG, which increased by
a total of 7.84% and 4.75% in B6 and B9 insects when
compared to WT insects. A heat map demonstrating the
relative abundances of lipids with significant between-
treatment differences revealed that B6 and B9 insects had
lower levels of most TG species compared to WT insects. In
contrast, both B6 and B9 insects had higher levels of PC
and DGDG species than WT insects ( Figure 3 B and T able
S6 in Supporting Information). The proportions of other
lipid classes, such as PE, PS, SM and DG, were relatively
stable across WT , B6 and B9 insects (T able S6 in Sup-
porting Information). These results suggest that TG is
converted to PC and DGDG when BPH insects were fed on
resistant rice. A similar transformation (TG to GP) has also
been observed in zebrafish larvae, and the transformation is
promoted by Wnt/Myc activity in a Ras-dependent manner
( Y ao et al., 2018 ) .

When changes in TG, PC and DGDG fatty acids were
analyzed, we discovered that the decreased levels of TG li-
pids in B6 and B9 were mainly explained by a reduction in
saturated fatty acyls (SF A), monounsaturated fatty acyls
(MUF A) containing C14, C16 and C18, and fatty acids
containing C18:2 ( Figure 4 D). W e also detected a substantial
increase in levels of the C18:2 PC in BPHs fed on resistant
rice, although this change was not statistically significant
( P =0.265 in B6 and P =0.316 in B9) due to lar ge variations
within the WT group ( Figure 4 E). The contents of other PC
fatty acids did not significantly diffe r among the tested BPH
insects, with the exception of increased levels of 36:2p in B9
relative to the other BPH insects ( Figure 4 E). In addition, we
analyzed the relative abundances of SF A, MUF A, diunsatu-
rated fatty acyls (DUF A), and polyunsaturated fatty acyls
(PUF A) in B6 and B9 relative to WT ( Figure 4 F). Notably ,
the decrease in TG fatty acids with diffe rent saturation levels
in B6 and B9 BPHs relative to WT insects coincided with an
increase in DGDG DUF A and PUF A in the B6 and B9 in-
sects ( Figure 4 G). Long-chain TG fatty acids (12<C<22)
were less abundant in both B6 and B9 insects relative to WT
insects, while B9 insects showed significantly higher levels
of very-long-chain fatty acids (C>21) than the other analyzed
insects (B6 and WT) ( Figure 4 G). In addition, B6 and B9
insects demonstrated elevated levels of long-chain DGDG
fatty acids when compared to WT insects ( Figure 4 G). The
B6 and B9 insects showed higher levels of PC long-chain
fatty acids and DUF A relative to WT insects, but no sig-
nificant difference was detected due to lar ge variations
among WT samples (Figure S5 in Supporting Information).
In summary , BPH insects fed on resistant rice (NIL- Bph6
and NIL- Bph9 ) demonstrated notable changes in the levels
of TG, PC and DGDG fatty acids.
Feeding on res istant plants altered the expre ssion of
genes related to lipid metabolism in BPHs

changes in lipid metabolism observed in BPHs fed on re-
sistant rice, we sequenced total RNA from BPH insects fed
on resistant (NIL- Bph6 and NIL- Bph9 ) and susceptible rice

platform. T ranscriptomic analyses were conducted on four
biological replicates from each of the three treatments (WT ,
B6 and B9) to profile transcriptional changes in BPH insects
fed on three diffe rent genotypes of rice. More than 636
million raw reads were obtained from these 12 transcriptome
libraries, with 48.3 to 59.1 million raw reads of 150 bp in
average length generated for each library ( T able 1 ). W e ret-

Our lipidomics analysis revealed that the total TG content, as
well as the contents of most TG species, decreased when
BPH insects were fed on resistant rice (NIL-Bph6 and NIL-
Bph9). Moreover , BPH insects fed on resistant rice showed
increased contents of PC and DGDG relative to WT insects.
This is a noteworthy finding because both of these com-
pounds are important components of membrane lipids.
Therefore, it was deduced that BPH insects fed on resistant
rice use TG as an energy source for maintaining growth and
ensuring survival. As shown in Figure 6B, we detected sig-
nificantly higher expression levels of three genes that encode

susceptible rice. Among these genes was brummer, which
encodes a lipase that participates in TG hydrolysis and has
previously been reported to be associated with lipid mobi-

interested in investigating whether the altered lipid mobili-

DISCUSSION
It has been estimated that herbivorous insects are responsible
for destroying up to 20% of the world’ s total annual crop
production. The BPH is a devastating insect pest for rice
plants; for this reason, we focused on providing new in-
formation about how rice plants defend against BPH in-
festation and how BPHs can adapt to resistant genotypes of
rice. In the current study , we combined mass-spectrometry-
based lipidomics with RNA-seq and RNA interference
techniques to investigate how lipid metabolism in BPHs
changed in response to host plant resistance. T o the best of
our knowledge, this is the first report of the complete BPH
lipidomic profile, and the present results can serve as a
biochemical resource for exploring the interactions between
BPH insects and the host plant.
The current study revealed that BPH insects fed on re-
sistant rice plants transformed TG to PC and DGDG; this
metabolic shift significantly altered the fatty acid composi-
tions of each of these lipid classes. In addition, ingestion of
resistant rice phloem noticeably modified the expression of
genes related to lipid metabolism, and the expression chan-
ges were particularly evident for genes whose encoded
products participate in fatty acid biosynthesis and elongation.

Plants have evolved elaborate protection systems that in-
clude physical barriers against insects as well as the pro-
duction of repellent, antinutritive or toxic compounds.
Antixenosis and antibiosis are common in rice plants that
carry one or more of the BPH resistance genes. Antibiosis
inhibits BPH feeding through multiple mechanisms. For
example, sieve tube sealing is a common mechanism which
protects against phloem feeders; more specifically , callose
deposition on the sieve plates occludes the sieve tubes to
inhibit continuous feeding by BPHs (Hao et al., 2008).
Protein plugging is a mechanism for sealing phloem sieve
pores during the resistance response to aphids, possibly
working in rice to BPH. Guo et al. (2018) recently reported
that 931 1-Bph6-NIL plants have thicker cell walls than 931 1
plants, which may be an ef fective guard against penetration
by BPH stylets. Furthermore, it has been shown that pro-
teinase inhibitor (PI) expression is induced by BPH in-
festation (Du et al., 2009). It may interfere with BPH
digestion (W eng et al., 2003; W ang et al., 2005; Y ang et al.,
2005; Du et al., 2009). These antibiosis factors prevent BPH
from feeding, resulting in the insect death from starvation,
and reductions of survival rate and reproduction. The current
study verified that NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 rice plants in-
hibited BPH feeding, resulting in decreased lipid contents
and body weight gain among the insects. W e propose that
decreased feeding on the resistant NIL rice plants leads to
enhanced lipolysis to provide energy for cell proliferation,
body maintenance, and growth.
W e also analyzed lipidomic changes in BPHs that were
fed on resistant rice plants using mass spectrometry . W e
observed changes in the composition of various lipid clas-
ses, and found that the stress of feeding on resistant plants
modified the prevalence and fatty acid chain length of
certain lipid species. In the present study , we identified 828
lipid metabolites in BPHs and found that feeding on re-
sistant rice plants promoted the transformation of TG to PC
and DGDG. Moreover , the expression levels of certain
genes involved in these transformations changed sig-
nificantly in BPH insects fed on resistant rice relative to
those fed on WT rice. For example, we noticed the up-
regulation of brummer, lipase and ABHD4, all of which
encode products that are responsible for the hydrolysis of
TG, along with the down-regulation of dgat1, which has
been linked to the transformation of DG to TG. This finding
may well explain the decreased TG contents observed in
BPH insects fed on resistant rice genotypes relative to those
fed on WT rice plants. In insects, glycogen and TG are
major sources of energy , and TG are mainly stored within
adipocytes and generally function as an energy reserve re-
levant to growth, reproduction, prolonged flight and star-
vation stress (Buckner and Hagen, 2003; Arrese and
Soulages, 2010; W ang et al., 2010). Results from both fruit
beetles (Pachnoda sinuata) and migratory locusts (Locusta
migratoria migratorioides) have revealed that glycogen
serves as a primary fuel during the initial stage of starva-
tion, but as starvation progresses, lipid mobilization be-
comes the dominant ener gy source for metabolic demands
(Hill and Goldsworthy , 1970; Auerswald and Gäde, 2000).
Research into how insects derive ener gy to power critical
metabolic processes during starvation conditions has shown
that grasshoppers (Romalea micr optera), cockroaches
(Gr omphador hina portentosa), and beetles (Zophobis
morio) rely heavily on lipids when exposed to the stress of
starvation (McCue et al., 2015). Thus, we propose that
feeding on resistant NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 rice plants
accelerates the rate at which BPHs break down TG reserves
to provide energy for metabolic processes.
The increased expression of plb1 and decreased expression
of lpcat3 led to a decrease in PC content. This finding in-
dicates that the increased PC contents in BPH insects fed on
resistant rice was not primarily due to the conversion of LPC
to PC. The increased PC contents in BPH insects fed on
resistant rice plants may be a result of other major PC bio-
synthetic pathways, e.g., the CDP-choline and/or methyla-
tion pathway (V ance and V ance, 2004; Cole et al., 2012). The
up-regulation of glct5 promoted the transformation of
MGDG to DGDG. PC, as the primary component of eu-
karyotic cell membranes and the precursor of several sig-
naling molecules (T ronchère et al., 1994; van Meer et al.,
2008), is of great physiological significance. Moreover , PC
has been suggested to be critical to the control of cell growth
and proliferation (Jackowski, 1994; Jackowski, 1996), as
well as apoptosis (Cui et al., 1996; Baburina and Jackowski,
1998; Anthony et al., 1999). DGDG, which is a major
component of the thylakoid membrane of chloroplasts, may
be a direct product of FF A hydrolysis or an indirect product
of the hydrolysis of galactose moieties from galactolipids
(Christeller et al., 201 1). The elevated PC and DGDG levels
in the BPH nymphs that ingested NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9
plant phloem indicate that these insects still managed to
regulate cell proliferation and body growth, although these
processes were clearly inhibited when compared to the
growth rates of BPH nymphs fed on susceptible rice plants
(Figure 1). W e have provided detailed lipidomic profiles for
BPH insects fed on three different rice genotypes (two BPH
resistant and one BPH susceptible), and found that the in-
gestion of resistant rice plant phloem promoted the lipolysis
of TG reserves to provide energy for cell division and body
growth.
Our data showed that the most abundant TG fatty acids in
the BPHs included C16:0, C18:0, C18:1 and C18:2, as pre-
viously reported for Melanogryllus Desertus (Bozkuş, 2003),
Acheta domesticus (Grapes et al., 1989), Dolycoris baccar-
um (Bashan and Cakmak, 2005), Piezodorus lituratus (Ba-
shan and Cakmak, 2005) and several other insects

(Thompson, 1973; Stanley-Samuelson and Dadd, 1983). It is
important to state that the degree of saturation and chain
length of a fatty acid is essential for its physiological func-
tions (Guillou et al., 2010). The presented data indicate that
BPHs fed on NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 rice plants had re-
duced concentrations of most TG lipid species and long-
chain fatty acids with diffe rent degrees of saturation, espe-
cially SF A and MUF A containing C14, C16 and C18, as well
as the unsaturated C18:2, relative to BPHs fed on WT plants
(Figure 4). Nevertheless, B9 insects show increased levels of
very-long-chain fatty acids relative to WT insects due to the
increased expression of a fatty acid elongation enzyme
(Figure 4 and Figure 6C). It has been shown that TG fatty
acids in the brown and retroperitoneal adipose tissue of rats
are selectively mobilized based on molecular structure dur -
ing fasting-induced energy depletion (Raclot and Groscolas,
1995; Groscolas and Herzber g, 1997). The current study
revealed that the ingestion of resistant rice phloem by BPH
insects extensively reduced the levels of all TG fatty acids.
Conversely , in the case of PC, B6 and B9 insects showed a
substantial increase in C18:2 relative to WT insects, although
this change did not reach statistical significance. The sub-
stantial increase in C18:2 PC lipids in B6 and B9 insects
might be a result of complicated physiological factors. C18:2
phospholipids are common in insects and usually function as
a structural component of cell membranes to maintain
fluidity and stability (Howard and Stanley-Samuelson, 1990;
Stanley-Samuelson et al., 1990). C18:2 is also a precursor to
arachidonic acid (20:4), which is a PUF A precursor to ei-
cosanoids. Prostaglandins (PGs), epoxyeicosatrienoic acids,
and various lipoxygenase (LOX) metabolites have been re-
cognized as the three major groups of eicosanoids (Stanley ,
2006), with each of these eicosanoids having important
biological functions in the regulation of physiological pro-
cesses. For example, PGs are involved in stimulating egg-
laying behavior in crickets (Acheta domesticus) (Destephano
et al., 1974), controlling ovarian follicle development in the
silkmoth (Bombyx mori) (Machado et al., 2007), and reg-
ulating vitellogenesis in Rhodnius pr olixus (Medeiros et al.,
2002). Furthermore, it has been established that PGs play an
essential role in regulating oviposition in N. lugens (Uchida
et al., 1987).
Our results also revealed that BPH insects fed on three
diffe rent rice genotypes (NIL-Bph6, NIL-Bph9 and 931 1)
significantly differed in the transcriptional level. Most of the
transcriptional changes in BPHs fed on resistant rice plants
were related to the down-regulation of growth and devel-
opmental processes, along with complex modifications to
lipid metabolism processes. The pathways of fatty acid me-
tabolism and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis were sig-
nificantly enriched according to the pathway analysis results
for both up- and down-regulated DEGs. This suggests that
changes in BPH lipid metabolism brought about by host
resistance are complicated and include the up-regulation of
certain genes and the down-regulation of others. This may be
explained by the fact that BPHs include fatty acids re-
presenting diffe rent lipid classes, with the compositions of
these lipid classes varying greatly between insects fed on
resistant plants and insects fed on susceptible plants (Figures
3 and 4).
In D. melanogaster, brummer silencing has been shown to
decrease both the rate of lipolysis and energy utilization,
eventually leading to obesity in flies (Grönke et al., 2005;
Grönke et al., 2007). In Glossina morsitans, bmm knock-
down resulted in reduced hemolymph lipid levels and sig-
nificantly delayed oocyte/early progeny development
(Attardo et al., 2012), while the loss of bmm activity in N.
lugens led to obesity , retarded ovarian development, and
impaired lipid mobilization in fat bodies (Lu et al., 2018b).
The current study showed that NlBmm-deficient insects fed
on susceptible rice (931 1) displayed increased feeding per -
formance and elevated TG levels, but a reduced survival rate,
relative to dsGFP-injected controls. Similar results were
found in the NlBmm-deficient insects fed on resistant NIL-
Bph6 rice plants. This provides evidence that NlBmm is re-
sponsible for lipid mobilization. Furthermore, we speculate
that NlBmm-deficient insects have a reduced ability to mo-
bilize fat reserves, which means that they must ingest more
sap from plants for ener gy and survival. A delicate balance
between lipogenesis and lipolysis regulates the total amount
of lipids in insects (Grönke et al., 2005). Based on our ex-
periments, the knockdown of NlBmm reduces the survival
rate of BPHs; the most plausible explanation for this finding
is that BPHs are unable to fully utilize lipid reserves, with the
excessive fat accumulation leading to alterations in meta-
bolic pathways. Experiments in D. melanogaster have de-
monstrated that bmm
1
mutant males lacking BMM lipase
activity show increased whole-body triglyceride levels, yet a
significantly reduced life span, compared to bmm
r ev
control
males (Grönke et al., 2005). The same result was found in
female D. melanogaster flies (W at et al., 2020). Moreover ,
flies exposed to a high fat diet (HFD) maintained an obese
phenotype consistent with an increased triglyceride storage,
but displayed decreased survival, stress tolerance and
climbing ability (Rivera et al., 2019; Heinrichsen and Had-
dad, 2012). NlBmm-deficient insects that ingested NIL-Bph9
phloem showed elevated honeydew production and sig-
nificant TG accumulation compared to the dsGFP insects fed
on the same plant. However , the two groups of insects did not
significantly diffe r in survival rate, BPH weight gain or
weight gain ratio. The disparities in survival rate, BPH
weight gain and weight gain ratio between BPHs fed on NIL-
Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 plants were probably due to the dif-
ferent BPH resistance levels of the two rice varieties. An-
other possibility is that the lipid mobilization in BPH insects
that ingested NIL-Bph9 phloem was meditated by other

genes related to TG lipolysis. In addition to brummer lipase-
dependent lipolysis, adipokinetic hormone (AKH)-mediated
lipolysis is another important lipolytic system involved in
TG mobilization in insects. AKH is a metabolic neuropeptide
with structural and functional similarities to mammalian
glucagon (Geminard et al., 2006; Bharucha et al., 2008). In
D. melanogaster, chronic AKH overexpression induces the
breakdown of lipid storage droplets and organismal fat stores
(Grönke et al., 2007), while Gryllus bimaculatus injected
with AKH demonstrates a decrease in the amount of lipids
stored in fat bodies as well as a reduction in terminal oocytes
(Lorenz, 2003). Moreover , the AKH/AKHR signaling sys-
tem has been reported to be crucial for acute lipid mobili-
zation in N. lugens (Lu et al., 2018a). Thus, we theorize that
the increased lipolysis in BPH insects that ingested NIL-
Bph9 phloem is mediated by the combined action of brum-
mer lipase-dependent and AKH pathways. Our data reveal
that the bmm-mediated lipolysis pathway has an important
function in lipid mobilization among BPHs that were fed on
resistant rice for 48 h.
In summary , we investigated the lipidomic response of
BPHs that were fed on resistant rice plants. Our results reveal
that the BPHs utilize TG stores to provide energy for cell
proliferation, body maintenance and growth with the over -
arching objective of surviving on a resistant rice plant. BPH
insects fed on resistant rice also demonstrate extensive
changes in lipid metabolism and down-regulation of genes
related to growth and development relative to BPH insects
fed on wild-type plants. Moreover , the presented results in-
dicate that the modifications in BPH lipid metabolism, i.e.,
lipid mobilization, caused by resistance stress are mediated
by the NlBmm gene. Our data constitute a valuable bio-
chemical resource for future investigations of BPH-host in-
teractions.
MA TERIALS AND METHODS
Plant materials and insects
Three rice varieties were used in this study: 931 1, NIL-Bph6,
and NIL-Bph9. 931 1 is a susceptible indica variety with no
BPH resistance genes. NIL-Bph6 carries the BPH resistance
gene Bph6 while NIL-Bph9 carries the BPH resistance gene
Bph9 (Zhao et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2018). The rice plants
were grown in 9-cm-diameter plastic pots in a greenhouse
((26±0.5)°C, 16:8 h light: dark photoperiod). BPH insects
(biotype 1) were reared on the susceptible rice variety TN1
under the same environmental conditions.
T wo-host choice test
A two-host choice test was performed to evaluate the host
selection behavior of BPH insects on 931 1, NIL-Bph6 and
NIL-Bph9 rice plants. A susceptible and a resistant rice
seedling were grown on opposite sides of the same plastic
cup (9 cm×12 cm). At the four-l eaf stage, twenty third-in-
star nymphs were placed in the center of cups containing
rice seedlings, which were completely covered with nylon
mesh. The cups were placed in a greenhouse ((26±0.5)°C,
16:8 h light: dark photoperiod) to prevent the artificial in-
terference. The number of BPH nymphs that had settled on
each plant was recorded 3, 6, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 120 h after
release. A total of ten cups were analyzed for each paired
group.
Honeydew excr etion and BPH weight gain measure-
ments
Honeydew excretion and BPH weight gain measurements
were performed following the method of Zhao et al. (2016)
with slight modifications. Briefly , 931 1, NIL-Bph6 and
NIL-Bph9 rice plants were grown in plastic cups
(9 cm×12 cm), with one plant per cup. Fourth-instar BPH
nymphs and newly emerged female adults were measured
for honeydew excretion, weight gain and weight gain ratio.
BPH insects at both growth stages were measured using an
electronic balance (AUW120D, Shimadzu, Japan). Each
insect was introduced into a pre-weighed (recorded as W1)
parafilm sachet (2 cm×2.5 cm) that was then fixed on the
leaf sheath of a four-week-ol d rice plant 1 cm above the
soil. After 48 h of feeding, the insects were removed care-
fully from the sachets and each individual was re-weighed.
The total weight of the sachet containing the honeydew was
recorded as W2. BPH weight gain was calculated based on
weight changes of the BPH insect, while weight of the
excreted honeydew was calculated as W2-W1. The BPH
weight gain relative to the corresponding initial weight of
each BPH insect was used to calculate the BPH weight gain
ratio. Each experiment was repeated three times with 20
BPHs per replicate.
BPH survival rate
The BPH survival rate was determined using a method pre-
sented by Hu et al. (2018) with slight modifications. 931 1,
NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9 rice plants were grown in plastic
cups (9 cm×12 cm) (one plant per cup) under natural con-
ditions. At an age of one month, each rice plant was in-
dividually covered with an inverted transparent plastic cup
(9 cm×12 cm) that had a hole at the center of the base to
allow the plant to grow normally . The upper plastic cup was
perforated all around for air exchange. Once the set-up was
established, 10 third-instar nymphs were released to infest
the plants. The number of surviving BPH nymphs in each
cup was recorded daily for a total of 10 days after the in-
troduction of the insects. The survival rates were then cal-

culated as the number of surviving nymphs in each cup re-
lative to the number of initially released insects (10). The
experiment was repeated five times.
Fecundity analysis
The fecundity analysis was performed according to the
method of Xu et al. (2017) with several modifications. A
brachypterous female adult within 24 h of emerge nce was
paired with a brachypterous male adult, and the group was
introduced into a plastic tube (3 cm×10 cm) that was vented
at both ends and perforated all around for air exchange. The
tube was then sleeved onto a fresh one-month-old rice plant,
with the top covered with absorbent cotton wool to confine
the insects within the tube. The plants were maintained in a
greenhouse ((26±0.5)°C, 16:8 h light: dark photoperiod).
The newly hatched nymphs was counted and moved out of
the plastic tube every day . After seven days, the two adult
insects, if still alive, were carefully removed from the plastic
tube and the number of unhatched eggs was counted through
dissecting leaf sheaths under a stereomicroscope. A total of
fifteen pairs of brachypterous adults were tested on each rice
variety with three biological replicates.
Staining lipid dr oplets with Nile r ed
T o visualize the abdominal fat bodies of the BPH nymphs,
we carefully removed the dorsal epidermis of the insects
and fixed it in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room
temperature. Images were taken using a stereomicroscope.
Lipid accumulation in the fat bodies was assessed by Nile
red staining (Greenspan et al., 1985). More specifically , fat
body tissues were dissected in PBS and fixed in 4% par-
aformaldehyde overnight at 4°C. The tissues were then
washed three times with PBS and stained with Nile red
(Sigma Aldrich, USA) at a concentration of 15 µg mL
−1
for
3 h, after which the staining solution was removed by
dipping three times in PBS. Next, the fat body tissues were
incubated with 1 mg mL
−1
DAPI (D1306, Thermo Fisher
Scientific, USA) for nuclei staining and rinsed three times
with PBS. Subsequent images were obtained with a con-
focal microscope (Fluoview FV1000, Olympus Corpora-
tion, Japan). A total of ten fat body cells from three
individual insects fed on each tested plant were analyzed in
the lipid storage assay , and the Nile red-positive areas of fat
body cells were quantified using ImageJ software. The
value describing average lipid storage of BPHs fed on 931 1
was set as 1.
T riglyceride assay
Fourth-instar nymphs of BPH insects were placed onto four-
leaf stage resistant (NIL-Bph6 and NIL-Bph9) and suscep-
tible (931 1) rice plants at a density of eight insects per
seedling. After feeding for 48 h, the insects from each
treatment were collected separately and weighed, including
three replicates, after which they were immersed in liquid
nitrogen for the biochemical analysis of triglyceride content.
BPH insects collected from the NIL-Bph6, NIL-Bph9, and
931 1 plants were designated as B6, B9, and WT , respec-
tively . Each sample was homogenized thoroughly and then
dissociated in dissociation solution for 15 min. The org a-
nismal triglyceride content of BPH insects was then quan-
tified using an enzymatic triglyceride assay kit (Applygen
T echnologies Inc., Beijing, China) following the manu-
facturer ’ s instructions. The experiments included three bio-
logical replicates from each group.
Lipid extraction and lipidome pr ofiling by LC-MS/MS
Three groups of fourth-instar BPH nymphs representing each
treatment were collected after they were fed on rice plants for
48 h. The collected samples were frozen in liquid nitrogen
and ground, after which 50 mg of the powder was homo-
genized in 400 µL of 75% methanol and sonicated in an ice-
cold ultrasonic bath for 15 min. Next, 1mL ice-cold methyl
tert-butyl ether (MTBE) was added, followed by mixing at
4°C for 1 h and 15 min of sonication. In the following step,
250 μL of water was added, the mixture was vortexed for
1 min and allowed to sit still for 20 min before centrifugation
at 14,000×g and 4°C for 15 min. The supernatant was con-
centrated and dried under a SpeedV ac concentrator (Thermo
Fisher Scientific). The dried extract was resuspended in
isopropanol / methanol (1:1, v/v) for subsequent UHPLC-
MS/MS analysis.
The lipid profiling was performed at Shanghai Bioprofile
T echnology Company Ltd. (Shanghai). Lipid extracts were
analyzed using a UHPLC Ultimate 3000 system (Thermo
Fisher Scientific) coupled to a hybrid Q Exactive Plus Or -
bitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equip-
ped with an ESI source. The lipid separation was performed
using a Hypersil GOLD C18 column (100 mm×2.1 mm,
1.9 µm) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the following mo-
bile phase settings: buf fer A was prepared by dissolving
0.77 g of ammonium acetate in 40% (v/v) water and 60% (v/
v) acetonitrile; while buf fer B was 10% (v/v) acetonitrile and
90% (v/v) isopropanol. The lipids were eluted within 18 min
at a flow rate of 300 µL min
−1
. The orbitrap mass analyzer
was operated in positive and negative ion modes (+3 kV and
−2.5 kV , respectively). The MS conditions were: heater
temperature, 300°C; sheath gas flow rate, 45 arb; aux gas
flow rate, 15 arb; sweep gas flow rate, 1 arb; capillary
temperature, 350°C; S-Lens RF Level, 50%; scan ranges,
200–1,500 amu.

Lipid species identification and quantification
The lipid species were identified and quantified using a
method described by Breitkopf et al. (2017) with several
modifications. Briefly , once RA W data from the high re-
solution QExactive Plus were acquired, the MS1 peaks and
MS2 fragment ion peaks were integrated to generate chro-
matographic peak areas that could be aligned across the
sample set to identify lipid molecules. LipidSearch 4.1.30
software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to identify and
quantify lipid species according to accurate mass and frag-
ment matching. The key processing parameters were set as
follows: precursor tolerance, 5 ppm; product tolerance:
10 ppm; quantitation m/z tolerance: ±5 ppm; quantitation R T
(retention time) range: ±0.25 min; ion adducts: +H, +NH4
and +Na for positive ion mode, −H and +HCOO for negative
ion mode. The following parameters were relevant for
alignment: R T tolerance: 0.50 min; m-score threshold: 5.0;
main node filter: main isomer peak; T oprank filter: On; ID
quality filter: A, B and C. During peak alignment, the lipid
chromatographic peak areas were compared across the
sample set and relative quantification of individual lipid
species across the dataset was performed. Lipid ions with
significantly diffe rent levels across BPHs representing dif-
ferent treatment groups were identified using Student’ s t-test,
with the threshold for statistical significance setting at
P≤0.05.
RNA sequencing
Fourth-instar BPH nymphs were placed on four-leaf stage
rice plants at a density of eight insects per seedling. A total of
ten nymphs representing each treatment were collected 48 h
after introduction, then immediately immersed in liquid ni-
trogen and stored at −80°C. Each treatment contained four
biological replicates. T otal RNA was extracted from the
BPHs using the TRIzol® Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific)
according to the manufacturer ’ s instructions. An Agilent
2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent T echnologies, USA) was used to
assay the quality of RNA samples. The cDNA library con-
struction and RNA sequencing on Illumina HiSeq 4000
platform were conducted following the manufacturer ’ s pro-
tocols (Illumina, USA). The raw reads were filtered by re-
moving adapters, short reads and low-quality sequences to
obtain clean data.
Differential gene expre ssion analysis
The expression levels of genes were calculated and nor -
malized using the RPKM (reads per kilobase of exon model

DEGs were detected using the edgeR package (Robinson et
al., 2010) with the absolute value of log
2
FC≥1 and P<0.05
serving as thresholds. The GO classification system (http://
www .geneontology .or g/) was used to determine the possible
functions of all of the detected DEGs. The functional clas-
sification and GO functional enrichment analyses of identi-
fied DEGs were performed with WEGO and Goatools
software, respectively (Klopfenstein et al., 2018; Y e et al.,
2018). Pathway enrichment analyses of DEGs were con-
ducted using KOBAS (http://kobas.cbi.pku.edu.cn/home.do)
(Xie et al., 201 1). W e applied P≤0.05 as the threshold for
significantly enriched GO and KEGG pathways.
Real-time quantitative PCR
T otal RNA (1 µg) was isolated for first-strand cDNA
synthesis using a PrimeScript R T reagent Kit with gDNA

The real-time quantitative PCR reaction was performed on
the SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad, USA) and CFX96
T ouch™ Real-T ime System (Bio-Rad) according to the
manufacturer ’ s protocol. The relative expression levels of
the selected DEGs were determined using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method
with the housekeeping gene actin serving as the internal
control. Three independent biological replicates were used in
each experiment.
